groups.name: Gosanke
groups.about: The Big Three. They dominate shows and most serious collections. Learn to tell them apart and the rest gets much easier.

groups.name: Utsurimono
groups.about: Black base with exactly one other colour wrapping it. Two colours, not three.

groups.name: Bekko
groups.about: The reverse of Utsuri: a solid base colour with small black stepping-stone spots on the back only.

groups.name: Asagi & Shusui
groups.about: Blue, net-scaled fish with red on the flanks. Asagi is the oldest variety; Shusui is its scaleless descendant.

groups.name: Koromo & Goshiki
groups.about: Robed koi: a darker reticulation laid over the red of a Kohaku-type pattern.

groups.name: Hikarimono
groups.about: Metallic koi. Ogon and its relatives: one shining colour, sometimes with a scale pattern.

groups.name: Hikari-moyo & Utsuri
groups.about: Metallic skin carrying two or more colours: metallic versions of the classic patterns.

groups.name: Kawarimono
groups.about: The 'odd' class: every non-metallic koi that fits no other class. Chagoi, Soragoi, Kumonryu and friends.

groups.name: Tancho
groups.about: One round red spot on the head and nothing else. Named after the red-crowned crane.

groups.name: Scales & forms
groups.about: Not varieties: these describe how a fish is built. Any of them can be combined with almost any variety.

grades.note: Rough US retail bands, by size and grade. Bands, not quotes, and deliberately wide: individual fish vary enormously. Ask B&M what is actually in the greenhouse.

varieties.name: Kohaku
varieties.blurb: Red on a pure white ground, and no black anywhere. One black speck and it is something else. The benchmark variety.
varieties.fact: "Koi begin and end with Kohaku" is the hobby's oldest saying. The 2021 All Japan Grand Champion was a 102 cm Kohaku.

varieties.name: Taisho Sanke
varieties.blurb: Kohaku plus black, but the black sits above the lateral line and never on the head. A Kohaku wearing punctuation.
varieties.fact: "Sanke" is not short for Sanshoku. It fossilises 三毛, "three-hair", the same word as mikeneko, the calico cat.

varieties.name: Showa Sanshoku
varieties.blurb: A black fish with red and white on it. The tell: Showa has black on the head and wrapping the body. Sanke does not.
varieties.fact: First bred in 1927 by Hoshino Shigekichi, but the Showa you can buy is really a 1964 fish. The originals had a grey ground.

varieties.name: Shiro Utsuri
varieties.blurb: Black base with exactly one other colour wrapping it: white (Shiro), red (Hi) or yellow (Ki). Two colours, not three.
varieties.fact: Utsuri means "reflection": the white and black mirror each other across the body.

varieties.name: Hi Utsuri
varieties.blurb: Black wrapping a red-orange ground. Deep, even red is hard to get against heavy black, so a good one stands out.
varieties.fact: Hi (緋) is the scarlet used across koi names: higoi, the red carp, is where colour breeding started.

varieties.name: Ki Utsuri
varieties.blurb: Black over yellow. The rarest of the three Utsuri, and the oldest: the yellow line predates the white one.
varieties.fact: Ki Utsuri appeared before Shiro Utsuri, but the yellow is hard to fix, so they stay uncommon.

varieties.name: Shiro Bekko
varieties.blurb: A clean white fish with small black spots along the back, and none on the head. Simple, crisp, often underrated.
varieties.fact: Bekko means "tortoiseshell". Take the red off a Sanke and a Shiro Bekko is what is left.

varieties.name: Aka Bekko
varieties.blurb: Solid red body with black stepping-stone spots on the back. Bold from across the pond.
varieties.fact: The difference from Hi Utsuri: Bekko black sits on top as spots, Utsuri black wraps around the body.

varieties.name: Asagi
varieties.blurb: Blue net-patterned back with red running along the flanks and into the fins. The oldest variety, closest to the wild ancestor.
varieties.fact: The only variety with no founder and no date. Japanese sources openly say its origin was never written down.

varieties.name: Shusui
varieties.blurb: A scaleless Asagi: smooth sky-blue back with one neat row of mirror scales down the spine, red on the sides.
varieties.fact: Not a Niigata fish at all. Made in Tokyo in the 1910s by a goldfish dealer, from German scaleless carp.

varieties.name: Goshiki
varieties.blurb: "Five colours": a Kohaku pattern laid over a reticulated blue-black net. Darkens and lightens with the seasons.
varieties.fact: The same Goshiki can look almost black in cold water and nearly Kohaku-bright in summer.

varieties.name: Ai Goromo
varieties.blurb: A Kohaku whose red scales are edged in indigo blue, like a robe thrown over the pattern.
varieties.fact: Ai is indigo: the dye that coloured Japanese work clothes for centuries.

varieties.name: Budo Goromo
varieties.blurb: "Grape robe": the red is overlaid with a darker reticulation so it reads as bunches of grapes. Uncommon and priced accordingly.
varieties.fact: One of the few varieties where the type itself, not just the grade, pushes the price up at small sizes.

varieties.name: Yamabuki Ogon
varieties.blurb: A single solid metallic colour with no pattern at all: here, bright yellow-gold. Ogon is the family; the colour names the fish.
varieties.fact: The founder fish was caught in 1921; Sawata Aoki's line took a quarter-century to fix the gold.

varieties.name: Platinum Ogon
varieties.blurb: Solid metallic white, like polished silver. Glows in a dark-bottomed pond and is easy to spot from across the yard.
varieties.fact: Metallic koi are judged on lustre over the head and fins, not pattern. There isn't one.

varieties.name: Aka Matsuba
varieties.blurb: "Pine cone": each scale is darkened in the centre, giving a pine-cone texture over a solid red base.
varieties.fact: The matsuba net appears on gold, red and white fish. The base colour gives the name.

varieties.name: Kujaku
varieties.blurb: "Peacock": a metallic body with a pine-cone scale net and red or orange markings over the top.
varieties.fact: One of the flashiest koi in sunlight. Best seen from above, the way koi are meant to be viewed.

varieties.name: Hariwake
varieties.blurb: Two metallic colours only: platinum with gold or orange patches. Clean, bright, two-tone.
varieties.fact: Add a pine-cone scale net and a Hariwake becomes a Kujaku.

varieties.name: Kin Showa
varieties.blurb: A Showa with metallic skin, so the black, red and white all shine. Dramatic in sunlight.
varieties.fact: Metallic skin tends to soften black, so a sharp-patterned Kin Showa is a breeding achievement.

varieties.name: Chagoi
varieties.blurb: Plain brown or tea-coloured. Deeply unfashionable, the friendliest fish in the pond, usually the first to hand-feed, and it teaches the others to.
varieties.fact: Chagoi grow big and calm. Many keepers add one first precisely to tame the rest.

varieties.name: Soragoi
varieties.blurb: "Sky carp": solid soft grey-blue with a fine net of scales. Quiet, friendly, and often grows huge.
varieties.fact: Soragoi crossed with Chagoi is one route to Ochiba Shigure.

varieties.name: Ochiba Shigure
varieties.blurb: "Autumn leaves on water". Copper or bronze over blue-grey. Understated, and it looks extraordinary in a planted pond.
varieties.fact: The name is a haiku image: fallen leaves drifting in a late-autumn shower.

varieties.name: Karashigoi
varieties.blurb: Solid mustard-yellow, non-metallic. A gentle giant: one of the biggest-growing koi you can buy.
varieties.fact: Karashi is Japanese mustard, the hot yellow kind served with oden.

varieties.name: Kigoi
varieties.blurb: Plain lemon-yellow, non-metallic. Rarer than it looks, because good even yellow is hard to breed.
varieties.fact: The red-eyed albino form, Akame Kigoi, is a collector's curiosity.

varieties.name: Benigoi
varieties.blurb: Solid deep red, nose to tail, non-metallic. Like a Kohaku with no white at all.
varieties.fact: Beni is the deep crimson of safflower dye; hi is the brighter scarlet. Both words are used for koi reds.

varieties.name: Kumonryu
varieties.blurb: A scaleless black-and-white fish that changes its pattern with the seasons and water temperature. No two years look alike.
varieties.fact: Named after the nine-dragon tattoo of a hero in Water Margin. The fish's swirls were said to resemble it.

varieties.name: Kikokuryu
varieties.blurb: "Sparkling black dragon": a metallic Kumonryu. Shining black and platinum, scaleless.
varieties.fact: Add red or orange and it becomes a Beni Kikokuryu, one of the most colourful modern koi.

varieties.name: Ghost koi
varieties.blurb: A koi × metallic wild-carp hybrid: dark, shimmering, and appears to fade in and out of the water. Hardy and fast-growing.
varieties.fact: Not a recognised show variety, but hugely popular in backyard ponds because ghosts are tough.

varieties.name: Tancho
varieties.blurb: One round red spot on the head and nothing else. If the body carries red too, it is a Maruten, not a Tancho.
varieties.fact: The tancho is Japan's red-crowned crane, and the spot echoes the Japanese flag. A perfectly round, centred spot is rare.

varieties.name: Kinginrin
varieties.blurb: Reflective "diamond" scales that can be added to almost any variety. Judged as its own class at shows.
varieties.fact: The 1929 Ginrin and the 1969 Diamond Ginrin are two separate events routinely merged into one.

varieties.name: Doitsu
varieties.blurb: Scaleless, with mirror scale rows along the back and flanks. Pattern edges read sharper without scale texture softening them.
varieties.fact: Doitsu means "German". Of the 30 mirror carp shipped from Munich in 1904, five fry survived. Four were female.

varieties.name: Butterfly / longfin
varieties.blurb: Long trailing fins. A Western favourite, and not a judged variety in Japan, where it is often cheaper rather than dearer.
varieties.fact: Developed in the 1980s by crossing koi with Indonesian longfin river carp.

varieties.name: Midorigoi
varieties.blurb: The green koi: a scaleless, yellow-green fish that glows like pond water in sunlight. Often fades to a duller yellow as it ages.
varieties.fact: Green is the one colour koi breeding almost never produces. Midorigoi come from crossing Shusui with Yamabuki Ogon.
